The age (in years) of a population is normally distributed with a mean of 36 and standard deviation of 12. The height (in cm) of the same population is also normally distributed with a mean of 160 and standard deviation of 10.

If the probability of age greater than 50 years is equal to the probability of height greater than hhh, the value of hhh (in cm) is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questionText: The age (in years) of a population is normally distributed with a mean of 36 and standard deviation of 12. The height (in cm) of the same population is also normally distributed with a mean of 160 and standard deviation of 10.If the probability of age greater than 50 years is equal to the probability of height greater than $h$ , the value of $h$ (in cm) is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Age distribution: Mean μa=36\mu_a = 36μa​=36, SD σa=12\sigma_a = 12σa​=12
Height distribution: Mean μh=160\mu_h = 160μh​=160, SD σh=10\sigma_h = 10σh​=10

Step 1 - Find z-score for age > 50:
z=50−3612=1412=1.16‾≈1.167z = \dfrac{50 - 36}{12} = \dfrac{14}{12} = 1.1\overline{6} \approx 1.167z=1250−36​=1214​=1.16≈1.167

Step 2 - The probability P(age > 50) = P(Z > 1.167)
This equals the same probability for height:
P(height>h)=P(Z>1.167)P(\text{height} > h) = P(Z > 1.167)P(height>h)=P(Z>1.167)

Step 3 - Find h using the same z-score:
h−16010=1.167\dfrac{h - 160}{10} = 1.16710h−160​=1.167
h=160+1.167×10=160+11.67=171.67 cmh = 160 + 1.167 \times 10 = 160 + 11.67 = \mathbf{171.67 \text{ cm}}h=160+1.167×10=160+11.67=171.67 cm
explanationText: Age distribution: Mean $\mu_a = 36$ , SD $\sigma_a = 12$ Height distribution: Mean $\mu_h = 160$ , SD $\sigma_h = 10$ Step 1 - Find z-score for age > 50: $z = \dfrac{50 - 36}{12} = \dfrac{14}{12} = 1.1\overline{6} \approx 1.167$ Step 2 - The probability P(age > 50) = P(Z > 1.167)This equals the same probability for height: $P(\text{height} > h) = P(Z > 1.167)$ Step 3 - Find h using the same z-score: $\dfrac{h - 160}{10} = 1.167$ $h = 160 + 1.167 \times 10 = 160 + 11.67 = \mathbf{171.67 \text{ cm}}$

questionText: Consider differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x$ with the condition $y = 0$ at $x = 0$ .The value of $y$ at $x = 1.0$ is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Given ODE: dydx+xy=x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = xdxdy​+xy=x, y(0)=0y(0) = 0y(0)=0

Step 1 - This is a linear first-order ODE. Rewrite:
dydx+xy=x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = xdxdy​+xy=x

Step 2 - Integrating factor (IF):
IF=e∫x dx=ex2/2IF = e^{\int x\,dx} = e^{x^2/2}IF=e∫xdx=ex2/2

Step 3 - Multiply both sides by IF:
ddx(y⋅ex2/2)=x⋅ex2/2\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y \cdot e^{x^2/2}\right) = x \cdot e^{x^2/2}dxd​(y⋅ex2/2)=x⋅ex2/2

Step 4 - Integrate both sides:
y⋅ex2/2=∫x⋅ex2/2 dxy \cdot e^{x^2/2} = \int x \cdot e^{x^2/2}\,dxy⋅ex2/2=∫x⋅ex2/2dx
Let t=x2/2t = x^2/2t=x2/2, dt=x dxdt = x\,dxdt=xdx:
=∫et dt=et+C=ex2/2+C= \int e^t\,dt = e^t + C = e^{x^2/2} + C=∫etdt=et+C=ex2/2+C

Step 5 - General solution:
y=1+Ce−x2/2y = 1 + Ce^{-x^2/2}y=1+Ce−x2/2

Step 6 - Apply initial condition y(0) = 0:
0=1+C⇒C=−10 = 1 + C \Rightarrow C = -10=1+C⇒C=−1
y=1−e−x2/2y = 1 - e^{-x^2/2}y=1−e−x2/2

Step 7 - Find y at x = 1:
y(1)=1−e−1/2=1−e−0.5=1−0.6065=0.39y(1) = 1 - e^{-1/2} = 1 - e^{-0.5} = 1 - 0.6065 = \mathbf{0.39}y(1)=1−e−1/2=1−e−0.5=1−0.6065=0.39
explanationText: Given ODE: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x$ , $y(0) = 0$ Step 1 - This is a linear first-order ODE. Rewrite: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x$ Step 2 - Integrating factor (IF): $IF = e^{\int x\,dx} = e^{x^2/2}$ Step 3 - Multiply both sides by IF: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y \cdot e^{x^2/2}\right) = x \cdot e^{x^2/2}$ Step 4 - Integrate both sides: $y \cdot e^{x^2/2} = \int x \cdot e^{x^2/2}\,dx$ Let $t = x^2/2$ , $dt = x\,dx$ : $= \int e^t\,dt = e^t + C = e^{x^2/2} + C$ Step 5 - General solution: $y = 1 + Ce^{-x^2/2}$ Step 6 - Apply initial condition y(0) = 0: $0 = 1 + C \Rightarrow C = -1$ $y = 1 - e^{-x^2/2}$ Step 7 - Find y at x = 1: $y(1) = 1 - e^{-1/2} = 1 - e^{-0.5} = 1 - 0.6065 = \mathbf{0.39}$

explanationText: Given: $\vec{V} = 3x^2yz\,\hat{i} - 5xy\,\hat{j} + 6yz^2\,\hat{k}$ Curl formula: $\nabla \times \vec{V} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \partial/\partial x & \partial/\partial y & \partial/\partial z \\ V_x & V_y & V_z \end{vmatrix}$ Components: $V_x = 3x^2yz,\ V_y = -5xy,\ V_z = 6yz^2$ $\hat{i}$ component: $\dfrac{\partial V_z}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial V_y}{\partial z} = \dfrac{\partial(6yz^2)}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial(-5xy)}{\partial z} = 6z^2 - 0 = 6z^2$ At (2,−1,1): $6(1)^2 = 6$ $\hat{j}$ component: $\dfrac{\partial V_x}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial V_z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial(3x^2yz)}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial(6yz^2)}{\partial x} = 3x^2y - 0 = 3x^2y$ At (2,−1,1): $3(4)(-1) = -12$ $\hat{k}$ component: $\dfrac{\partial V_y}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial V_x}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial(-5xy)}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial(3x^2yz)}{\partial y} = -5y - 3x^2z$ At (2,−1,1): $-5(-1) - 3(4)(1) = 5 - 12 = -7$ Curl = $6\hat{i} - 12\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$
explanationTex: \nabla \times \vec{V} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \partial/\partial x & \partial/\partial y & \partial/\partial z \\ V_x & V_y & V_z \end{vmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial V_z}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial V_y}{\partial z} = \dfrac{\partial(6yz^2)}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial(-5xy)}{\partial z} = 6z^2 - 0 = 6z^2
\dfrac{\partial V_x}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial V_z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial(3x^2yz)}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial(6yz^2)}{\partial x} = 3x^2y - 0 = 3x^2y
\dfrac{\partial V_y}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial V_x}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial(-5xy)}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial(3x^2yz)}{\partial y} = -5y - 3x^2z

f(x)=x3(−p3−0)−sin⁡x(6p3−0)+cos⁡x(6p2−(−p))f(x) = x^3(-p^3 - 0) - \sin x(6p^3 - 0) + \cos x(6p^2 - (-p))f(x)=x3(−p3−0)−sinx(6p3−0)+cosx(6p2−(−p))
=−p3x3−6p3sin⁡x+cos⁡x(6p2+p)= -p^3 x^3 - 6p^3 \sin x + \cos x(6p^2 + p)=−p3x3−6p3sinx+cosx(6p2+p)

Taking third derivative:
f(x)=−p3x3−6p3sin⁡x+(6p2+p)cos⁡xf(x) = -p^3 x^3 - 6p^3 \sin x + (6p^2 + p)\cos xf(x)=−p3x3−6p3sinx+(6p2+p)cosx
f′(x)=−3p3x2−6p3cos⁡x−(6p2+p)sin⁡xf'(x) = -3p^3 x^2 - 6p^3 \cos x - (6p^2+p)\sin xf′(x)=−3p3x2−6p3cosx−(6p2+p)sinx
f′′(x)=−6p3x+6p3sin⁡x−(6p2+p)cos⁡xf''(x) = -6p^3 x + 6p^3 \sin x - (6p^2+p)\cos xf′′(x)=−6p3x+6p3sinx−(6p2+p)cosx
f′′′(x)=−6p3+6p3cos⁡x+(6p2+p)sin⁡xf'''(x) = -6p^3 + 6p^3 \cos x + (6p^2+p)\sin xf′′′(x)=−6p3+6p3cosx+(6p2+p)sinx

At x=0x=0x=0: f′′′(0)=−6p3+6p3(1)+(6p2+p)(0)=−6p3+6p3=0f'''(0) = -6p^3 + 6p^3(1) + (6p^2+p)(0) = -6p^3 + 6p^3 = \mathbf{0}f′′′(0)=−6p3+6p3(1)+(6p2+p)(0)=−6p3+6p3=0

explanationText: Key observation: Expanding the determinant along Row 2 (constants), we get: $f(x) = 6 \cdot M_{21} + (-1) \cdot M_{22} + 0 \cdot M_{23}$ where $M_{ij}$ are cofactors.The third derivative $\dfrac{d^3}{dx^3}f(x)$ only acts on terms involving $x$ .Expanding along Row 1: $f(x) = x^3(-p^3 - 0) - \sin x(6p^3 - 0) + \cos x(6p^2 - (-p))$ $= -p^3 x^3 - 6p^3 \sin x + \cos x(6p^2 + p)$ Taking third derivative: $f(x) = -p^3 x^3 - 6p^3 \sin x + (6p^2 + p)\cos x$ $f'(x) = -3p^3 x^2 - 6p^3 \cos x - (6p^2+p)\sin x$ $f''(x) = -6p^3 x + 6p^3 \sin x - (6p^2+p)\cos x$ $f'''(x) = -6p^3 + 6p^3 \cos x + (6p^2+p)\sin x$ At $x=0$ : $f'''(0) = -6p^3 + 6p^3(1) + (6p^2+p)(0) = -6p^3 + 6p^3 = \mathbf{0}$ The result is 0, which is independent of p.

questionText: The eigenvalues of $[A] = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3.5 & 6 \\ 3.5 & 5 & 2 \\ 8 & 1 & 8.5 \end{bmatrix}$ are $\lambda_1 = -1.547$ , $\lambda_2 = 12.330$ , and $\lambda_3 = 4.711$ .The absolute value of the determinant of matrix $A$ is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Key property: The determinant of a matrix equals the product of its eigenvalues.

Given eigenvalues: λ1=−1.547, λ2=12.330, λ3=4.711\lambda_1 = -1.547,\ \lambda_2 = 12.330,\ \lambda_3 = 4.711λ1​=−1.547, λ2​=12.330, λ3​=4.711

Determinant:
∣det⁡(A)∣=∣λ1×λ2×λ3∣|\det(A)| = |\lambda_1 \times \lambda_2 \times \lambda_3|∣det(A)∣=∣λ1​×λ2​×λ3​∣
=∣(−1.547)×12.330×4.711∣= |(-1.547) \times 12.330 \times 4.711|=∣(−1.547)×12.330×4.711∣
=∣(−1.547)×58.090∣= |(-1.547) \times 58.090|=∣(−1.547)×58.090∣
=∣−89.86∣= |{-89.86}|=∣−89.86∣
=89.87= \mathbf{89.87}=89.87
explanationText: Key property: The determinant of a matrix equals the product of its eigenvalues.Given eigenvalues: $\lambda_1 = -1.547,\ \lambda_2 = 12.330,\ \lambda_3 = 4.711$ Determinant: $|\det(A)| = |\lambda_1 \times \lambda_2 \times \lambda_3|$ $= |(-1.547) \times 12.330 \times 4.711|$ $= |(-1.547) \times 58.090|$ $= |{-89.86}|$ $= \mathbf{89.87}$

Testing each option:

Difference = 6(x−2y)−24(x−2y)≠06(x-2y) - 24(x-2y) \neq 06(x−2y)−24(x−2y)=0

(C) u=cos⁡(x+y)u = \cos(x+y)u=cos(x+y):

Difference = 0 Valid solution

Difference =−sin⁡+4sin⁡=3sin⁡≠0= -\sin + 4\sin = 3\sin \neq 0=−sin+4sin=3sin=0
explanationText: The PDE is: $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} - \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0$ (Wave equation type)This is a hyperbolic PDE. General solution: $u = f(x+y) + g(x-y)$ Testing each option:(A) $u = (x+y)^5$ : $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = 20(x+y)^3$ , $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 20(x+y)^3$ Difference = 0 Valid solution(B) $u = (x-2y)^3$ : $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = 6(x-2y)$ , $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 4 \times 6(x-2y) = 24(x-2y)$ ... wait: $\dfrac{\partial^2}{\partial y^2}(x-2y)^3 = (-2)^2 \times 6(x-2y) = 24(x-2y)$ Difference = $6(x-2y) - 24(x-2y) \neq 0$ (C) $u = \cos(x+y)$ : $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = -\cos(x+y)$ , $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -\cos(x+y)$ Difference = 0 Valid solution(D) $u = \sin(x-2y)$ : $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = -\sin(x-2y)$ , $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -4\sin(x-2y)$ Difference $= -\sin + 4\sin = 3\sin \neq 0$

questionText: A fifth-degree polynomial in $x$ is defined for $x > 0$ . All coefficients of the polynomial are positive. The first derivative of the polynomial is obtained numerically at a point by using the first-order forward as well as the first-order backward difference methods. Identical step lengths are used for both methods.Following statements are made:(I) Forward difference method underestimates the true derivative.(II) Backward difference method overestimates the true derivative.Which one of the following options is CORRECT?

options.html: Both statements (I) and (II) are FALSE.

options.html: Statement (I) is FALSE and statement (II) is TRUE.
options.text: Statement (I) is FALSE and statement (II) is TRUE.

explanationHtml:
Given:
A fifth-degree polynomial with all positive coefficients:f(x)=a5x5+a4x4+a3x3+a2x2+a1x+a0(ai>0, x>0) f(x)=a_5x^5+a_4x^4+a_3x^3+a_2x^2+a_1x+a_0 \qquad (a_i>0,\ x>0) f(x)=a5​x5+a4​x4+a3​x3+a2​x2+a1​x+a0​(ai​>0, x>0)
We need to determine whether the first-order forward and backward difference approximations overestimate or underestimate the true derivative.

Step 1: Examine the second derivative

The first derivative isf′(x)=5a5x4+4a4x3+3a3x2+2a2x+a1 f'(x) = 5a_5x^4+4a_4x^3+3a_3x^2+2a_2x+a_1 f′(x)=5a5​x4+4a4​x3+3a3​x2+2a2​x+a1​
The second derivative isf′′(x)=20a5x3+12a4x2+6a3x+2a2 f''(x) = 20a_5x^3+12a_4x^2+6a_3x+2a_2 f′′(x)=20a5​x3+12a4​x2+6a3​x+2a2​
Since all coefficients are positive andx>0, x>0, x>0,we havef′′(x)>0. f''(x)>0. f′′(x)>0.
Therefore, the function is convex (concave upward).

Step 2: Forward difference approximation

The first-order forward difference formula isf′(x)≈f(x+h)−f(x)h. f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}. f′(x)≈hf(x+h)−f(x)​.
For a convex function,f(x+h)−f(x)h>f′(x). \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} > f'(x). hf(x+h)−f(x)​>f′(x).
Hence, the forward difference method overestimates the true derivative.

Therefore, Statement (I) is FALSE.

Step 3: Backward difference approximation

The first-order backward difference formula isf′(x)≈f(x)−f(x−h)h. f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}. f′(x)≈hf(x)−f(x−h)​.
For a convex function,f(x)−f(x−h)h<f′(x). \frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h} < f'(x). hf(x)−f(x−h)​<f′(x).
Hence, the backward difference method underestimates the true derivative.

Therefore, Statement (II) is FALSE.

Using Lagrange's interpolation formula:
P2(x)=y0⋅L0(x)+y1⋅L1(x)+y2⋅L2(x)P_2(x) = y_0 \cdot L_0(x) + y_1 \cdot L_1(x) + y_2 \cdot L_2(x)P2​(x)=y0​⋅L0​(x)+y1​⋅L1​(x)+y2​⋅L2​(x)

L2(x)=(x+2)(x−1)(2+2)(2−1)=(x+2)(x−1)4L_2(x) = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-1)}{(2+2)(2-1)} = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-1)}{4}L2​(x)=(2+2)(2−1)(x+2)(x−1)​=4(x+2)(x−1)​

At x = 0:
L0(0)=(−1)(−2)12=212=16L_0(0) = \dfrac{(-1)(-2)}{12} = \dfrac{2}{12} = \dfrac{1}{6}L0​(0)=12(−1)(−2)​=122​=61​
L1(0)=(0−4)−3=43L_1(0) = \dfrac{(0-4)}{-3} = \dfrac{4}{3}L1​(0)=−3(0−4)​=34​
L2(0)=(2)(−1)4=−24=−12L_2(0) = \dfrac{(2)(-1)}{4} = \dfrac{-2}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{2}L2​(0)=4(2)(−1)​=4−2​=−21​

P2(0)=28×16+4×43+16×(−12)P_2(0) = 28 \times \dfrac{1}{6} + 4 \times \dfrac{4}{3} + 16 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)P2​(0)=28×61​+4×34​+16×(−21​)
=286+163−8=143+163−8=303−8=10−8=2= \dfrac{28}{6} + \dfrac{16}{3} - 8 = \dfrac{14}{3} + \dfrac{16}{3} - 8 = \dfrac{30}{3} - 8 = 10 - 8 = \mathbf{2}=628​+316​−8=314​+316​−8=330​−8=10−8=2

questionText: An ordinary differential equation is given below: $x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6y$ Considering $a$ and $b$ as arbitrary constants, the general solution of the equation is

options.html: y(x)=ax3+bx2y(x) = ax^3 + \dfrac{b}{x^2}y(x)=ax3+x2b​
y(x)=ax2+bx3y(x) = ax^2 + \dfrac{b}{x^3}y(x)=ax2+x3b​
y(x)=ax2+bln⁡xy(x) = ax^2 + b\ln xy(x)=ax2+blnx
y(x)=ax3+bln⁡xy(x) = ax^3 + b\ln xy(x)=ax3+blnx

explanationHtml:
Given ODE: x2d2ydx2=6yx^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6yx2dx2d2y​=6y → \rightarrow → x2y′′−6y=0x^2 y'' - 6y = 0x2y′′−6y=0

This is an Euler-Cauchy equation. Assume y=xmy = x^my=xm:

y′=mxm−1,y′′=m(m−1)xm−2y' = mx^{m-1},\quad y'' = m(m-1)x^{m-2}y′=mxm−1,y′′=m(m−1)xm−2

Substituting:
x2⋅m(m−1)xm−2−6xm=0x^2 \cdot m(m-1)x^{m-2} - 6x^m = 0x2⋅m(m−1)xm−2−6xm=0
m(m−1)xm−6xm=0m(m-1)x^m - 6x^m = 0m(m−1)xm−6xm=0
[m(m−1)−6]xm=0[m(m-1) - 6]x^m = 0[m(m−1)−6]xm=0
m2−m−6=0m^2 - m - 6 = 0m2−m−6=0
(m−3)(m+2)=0(m-3)(m+2) = 0(m−3)(m+2)=0
m=3 or m=−2m = 3 \text{ or } m = -2m=3 or m=−2

General solution:
y(x)=ax3+bx−2=ax3+bx2y(x) = ax^3 + bx^{-2} = ax^3 + \dfrac{b}{x^2}y(x)=ax3+bx−2=ax3+x2b​
explanationText: Given ODE: $x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6y$ $\rightarrow$ $x^2 y'' - 6y = 0$ This is an Euler-Cauchy equation. Assume $y = x^m$ : $y' = mx^{m-1},\quad y'' = m(m-1)x^{m-2}$ Substituting: $x^2 \cdot m(m-1)x^{m-2} - 6x^m = 0$ $m(m-1)x^m - 6x^m = 0$ $[m(m-1) - 6]x^m = 0$ $m^2 - m - 6 = 0$ $(m-3)(m+2) = 0$ $m = 3 \text{ or } m = -2$ General solution: $y(x) = ax^3 + bx^{-2} = ax^3 + \dfrac{b}{x^2}$

questionText: It is given that $x$ and $y$ are integers in the following equation: $(x + y - 7)^2 + (y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0$ The value of $(x^3 + y^3)$ is ________ (in integer).
explanationHtml:
Given: (x+y−7)2+(y+3x−13)2=0(x + y - 7)^2 + (y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0(x+y−7)2+(y+3x−13)2=0

Key insight: Sum of two squares equals zero only when each square is zero.

(x+y−7)2=0⇒x+y=7⋯(1)(x + y - 7)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x + y = 7 \quad \cdots (1)(x+y−7)2=0⇒x+y=7⋯(1)
(y+3x−13)2=0⇒y+3x=13⋯(2)(y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow y + 3x = 13 \quad \cdots (2)(y+3x−13)2=0⇒y+3x=13⋯(2)

Solving the system:
Subtract (1) from (2):
(y+3x)−(x+y)=13−7(y + 3x) - (x + y) = 13 - 7(y+3x)−(x+y)=13−7
2x=6⇒x=32x = 6 \Rightarrow x = 32x=6⇒x=3

Substitute into (1): 3+y=7⇒y=43 + y = 7 \Rightarrow y = 43+y=7⇒y=4

Calculate x3+y3=33+43=27+64=91x^3 + y^3 = 3^3 + 4^3 = 27 + 64 = \mathbf{91}x3+y3=33+43=27+64=91
explanationText: Given: $(x + y - 7)^2 + (y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0$ Key insight: Sum of two squares equals zero only when each square is zero. $(x + y - 7)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x + y = 7 \quad \cdots (1)$ $(y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow y + 3x = 13 \quad \cdots (2)$ Solving the system:Subtract (1) from (2): $(y + 3x) - (x + y) = 13 - 7$ $2x = 6 \Rightarrow x = 3$ Substitute into (1): $3 + y = 7 \Rightarrow y = 4$ Calculate $x^3 + y^3 = 3^3 + 4^3 = 27 + 64 = \mathbf{91}$

questionText: A matrix is given as: $\begin{bmatrix} 9 & 15 \\ 15 & 50 \end{bmatrix}$ By performing Cholesky decomposition, $|l_{22}|$ of the lower triangular matrix is ______ (in integer).
explanationHtml:
Given matrix: A=[9151550]A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 15 \\ 15 & 50 \end{bmatrix}A=[915​1550​]

Cholesky decomposition: A=LLTA = LL^TA=LLT, where L=[l110l21l22]L = \begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0 \\ l_{21} & l_{22} \end{bmatrix}L=[l11​l21​​0l22​​]

Step 1 - Find l11l_{11}l11​:
l11=a11=9=3l_{11} = \sqrt{a_{11}} = \sqrt{9} = 3l11​=a11​​=9​=3

Step 2 - Find l21l_{21}l21​:
l21=a21l11=153=5l_{21} = \dfrac{a_{21}}{l_{11}} = \dfrac{15}{3} = 5l21​=l11​a21​​=315​=5

Step 3 - Find l22l_{22}l22​:
l22=a22−l212=50−25=25=5l_{22} = \sqrt{a_{22} - l_{21}^2} = \sqrt{50 - 25} = \sqrt{25} = 5l22​=a22​−l212​​=50−25​=25​=5

∣l22∣=5|l_{22}| = \mathbf{5}∣l22​∣=5
explanationText: Given matrix: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 15 \\ 15 & 50 \end{bmatrix}$ Cholesky decomposition: $A = LL^T$ , where $L = \begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0 \\ l_{21} & l_{22} \end{bmatrix}$ Step 1 - Find $l_{11}$ : $l_{11} = \sqrt{a_{11}} = \sqrt{9} = 3$ Step 2 - Find $l_{21}$ : $l_{21} = \dfrac{a_{21}}{l_{11}} = \dfrac{15}{3} = 5$ Step 3 - Find $l_{22}$ : $l_{22} = \sqrt{a_{22} - l_{21}^2} = \sqrt{50 - 25} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ $|l_{22}| = \mathbf{5}$

explanationHtml:
Given:

Using Bayes' Theorem:
Let B = event of drawing a black ball

P(B∣B2)=37≈0.4286P(B | B_2) = \dfrac{3}{7} \approx 0.4286P(B∣B2​)=73​≈0.4286

Total probability of black ball:
P(B)=P(B1)⋅P(B∣B1)+P(B2)⋅P(B∣B2)P(B) = P(B_1) \cdot P(B|B_1) + P(B_2) \cdot P(B|B_2)P(B)=P(B1​)⋅P(B∣B1​)+P(B2​)⋅P(B∣B2​)
P(B)=12×610+12×37=310+314=2170+1570=3670P(B) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{10} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{3}{14} = \dfrac{21}{70} + \dfrac{15}{70} = \dfrac{36}{70}P(B)=21​×106​+21​×73​=103​+143​=7021​+7015​=7036​

Probability black ball came from Bag I:
P(B1∣B)=P(B1)⋅P(B∣B1)P(B)=12×6103670=3103670=310×7036=210360=712≈0.58P(B_1|B) = \dfrac{P(B_1) \cdot P(B|B_1)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{10}}{\dfrac{36}{70}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{10}}{\dfrac{36}{70}} = \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{70}{36} = \dfrac{210}{360} = \dfrac{7}{12} \approx \mathbf{0.58}P(B1​∣B)=P(B)P(B1​)⋅P(B∣B1​)​=7036​21​×106​​=7036​103​​=103​×3670​=360210​=127​≈0.58

questionText: Pick the CORRECT eigenvalue(s) of the matrix [A] from the following choices. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 8 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
explanationHtml:
Let A=[6842] A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 8 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} A=[64​82​]
To find the eigenvalues, solve the characteristic equation: det⁡(A−λI)=0 \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 det(A−λI)=0
⇒det⁡([6−λ8 42−λ])=0 \Rightarrow \det\left( \begin{bmatrix} 6 - \lambda & 8 \ 4 & 2 - \lambda \end{bmatrix} \right) = 0 ⇒det([6−λ​8 4​2−λ​])=0
Use determinant formula: (6−λ)(2−λ)−32=0 (6 - \lambda)(2 - \lambda) - 32 = 0 (6−λ)(2−λ)−32=0
⇒λ2−8λ−20=0 \Rightarrow \lambda^2 - 8\lambda - 20 = 0 ⇒λ2−8λ−20=0
Solve the quadratic: λ=8±(−8)2+4(20)2=8±64+802=8±1442 \lambda = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{(-8)^2 + 4(20)}}{2} = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{64 + 80}}{2} = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{144}}{2} λ=28±(−8)2+4(20)​​=28±64+80​​=28±144​​
⇒λ=8±122 \Rightarrow \lambda = \frac{8 \pm 12}{2} ⇒λ=28±12​
So the eigenvalues are: λ1=8+122=10 \lambda_1 = \frac{8 + 12}{2} = 10 λ1​=28+12​=10
λ2=8−122=−2 \lambda_2 = \frac{8 - 12}{2} = -2 λ2​=28−12​=−2
explanationText: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 8 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ To find the eigenvalues, solve the characteristic equation: $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ $\Rightarrow \det\left( \begin{bmatrix} 6 - \lambda & 8 \ 4 & 2 - \lambda \end{bmatrix} \right) = 0$ Use determinant formula: $(6 - \lambda)(2 - \lambda) - 32 = 0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda^2 - 8\lambda - 20 = 0$ Solve the quadratic: $\lambda = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{(-8)^2 + 4(20)}}{2} = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{64 + 80}}{2} = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{144}}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \lambda = \frac{8 \pm 12}{2}$ So the eigenvalues are: $\lambda_1 = \frac{8 + 12}{2} = 10$ $\lambda_2 = \frac{8 - 12}{2} = -2$

explanationHtml:
To determine the order of a differential equation, we look at the highest-order derivative present.
Given:
d3ydx3+(d2ydx2)6+(dydx)4+y=0 \frac{d^3 y}{d x^3} + \left( \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2} \right)^6 + \left( \frac{d y}{d x} \right)^4 + y = 0 dx3d3y​+(dx2d2y​)6+(dxdy​)4+y=0
Now, identify the order of each derivative term:
d3ydx3\frac{d^3 y}{d x^3}dx3d3y​ - 3rd order
(d2ydx2)6\left( \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2} \right)^6(dx2d2y​)6 - 2nd order (power doesn't affect order)
(dydx)4\left( \frac{d y}{d x} \right)^4(dxdy​)4 - 1st order
yyy - 0th order (no derivative)

This statement is correct.

Statement (D):
If A and B are independent, then P(A∩B)=P(A)⋅P(B)P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)P(A∩B)=P(A)⋅P(B).

explanationText: We are given the second-order linear differential equation (after combining terms): $y'' + 0.8y' + 0.16y = 0$ with initial conditions: $y(0) = 3$ , $y'(0) = 4.5$ Step 1: Solve the characteristic equation The auxiliary equation is: $r^2 + 0.8r + 0.16 = 0$ Solve using the quadratic formula: $r = \frac{-0.8 \pm \sqrt{(0.8)^2 - 4(1)(0.16)}}{2(1)}$ $r = \frac{-0.8 \pm \sqrt{0.64 - 0.64}}{2} = \frac{-0.8}{2} = -0.4$ This is a repeated root: $r = -0.4$ Step 2: General solution $y(t) = (A + Bt)e^{-0.4t}$ Step 3: Apply initial conditions $y(0) = (A + B \cdot 0)e^{0} = A = 3$ So, $A = 3$ Now find $y'(t)$ : $y'(t) = \frac{d}{dt}[(A + Bt)e^{-0.4t}] = B e^{-0.4t} + (A + Bt)(-0.4)e^{-0.4t}$ $y'(t) = \left[B - 0.4(A + Bt)\right]e^{-0.4t}$ At $t = 0$ : $y'(0) = [B - 0.4(3)] \cdot 1 = B - 1.2 = 4.5$ So, $B = 4.5 + 1.2 = 5.7$ Step 4: Final solution $y(t) = (3 + 5.7t)e^{-0.4t}$ Step 5: Find $y(1)$ $y(1) = (3 + 5.7 \cdot 1)e^{-0.4 \cdot 1} = (8.7)e^{-0.4}$ $e^{-0.4} \approx 0.6703$ $y(1) \approx 8.7 \cdot 0.6703 \approx 5.83$ Final Answer: $y(1) = \boxed{5.8}$ (rounded off to 1 decimal place)

explanationText: To evaluate the limit: $\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(x - \sqrt{x^2 + x} \right)$ We rationalize the expression by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate: $\begin{aligned} x - \sqrt{x^2 + x} &= \frac{(x - \sqrt{x^2 + x}) \cdot (x + \sqrt{x^2 + x})}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} \ &= \frac{x^2 - (x^2 + x)}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} \ &= \frac{-x}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} \end{aligned}$ Now evaluate the limit: $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{-x}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} = \frac{-1}{1 + \sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{x}}}$ As $x \to \infty$ , $\frac{1}{x} \to 0$ , so we get: $\frac{-1}{1 + \sqrt{1}} = \frac{-1}{1 + 1} = \boxed{-\frac{1}{2}}$ Final Answer: $-\frac{1}{2}$

Multiply both sides by 2:

explanationText: Step 1: Let $x = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix}$ Then $Ax = b$ means: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 3 \ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \ b_2 \ b_3 \end{bmatrix}$ This leads to the system: $x_1 + x_2 = b_1 \quad \text{(1)}$ $x_1 + 3x_2 = b_2 \quad \text{(2)}$ $-2x_1 - 3x_2 = b_3 \quad \text{(3)}$ Step 2: From equation (1), solve for $x_1 = b_1 - x_2$ Substitute into equation (2): $(b_1 - x_2) + 3x_2 = b_2 \Rightarrow b_1 + 2x_2 = b_2$ So, $x_2 = \frac{b_2 - b_1}{2}$ and then $x_1 = \frac{3b_1 - b_2}{2}$ Step 3: Plug into equation (3) to ensure consistency: $-2x_1 - 3x_2 = b_3$ Substitute values: $-2\left( \frac{3b_1 - b_2}{2} \right) - 3\left( \frac{b_2 - b_1}{2} \right) = b_3$ Simplify: $- (3b_1 - b_2) - \frac{3(b_2 - b_1)}{2} = b_3$ $-3b_1 + b_2 - \frac{3b_2 - 3b_1}{2} = b_3$ $-3b_1 + b_2 - \frac{3b_2}{2} + \frac{3b_1}{2} = b_3$ $(-3b_1 + \frac{3b_1}{2}) + (b_2 - \frac{3b_2}{2}) = b_3$ $-\frac{3b_1}{2} - \frac{b_2}{2} = b_3$ Multiply both sides by 2: $-3b_1 - b_2 = 2b_3$ Rearranged: $3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 = 0$ Final Answer: (B) $3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 = 0$

explanationHtml:
Solution:
We are given:
Ax=λx A x = \lambda x Ax=λx
So, λ\lambdaλ is an eigenvalue of matrix AAA and xxx is its corresponding eigenvector

We are also told that:
B=A−2I B = A - 2I B=A−2I, where III is the identity matrix

Now we need to find the eigenvalue of BBB corresponding to the same eigenvector xxx

Step 1: Apply BBB on xxx:
Bx=(A−2I)x=Ax−2Ix Bx = (A - 2I)x = Ax - 2Ix Bx=(A−2I)x=Ax−2Ix
Bx=λx−2x=(λ−2)x Bx = \lambda x - 2x = (\lambda - 2)x Bx=λx−2x=(λ−2)x

Step 2: Since Bx=(λ−2)xBx = (\lambda - 2)xBx=(λ−2)x, this shows that xxx is also an eigenvector of BBB, with eigenvalue:
λB=λ−2 \lambda_B = \lambda - 2 λB​=λ−2

Final Answer: λ−2\lambda - 2λ−2
explanationText: Solution: We are given: $A x = \lambda x$ So, $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of matrix $A$ and $x$ is its corresponding eigenvectorWe are also told that: $B = A - 2I$ , where $I$ is the identity matrixNow we need to find the eigenvalue of $B$ corresponding to the same eigenvector $x$ Step 1: Apply $B$ on $x$ : $Bx = (A - 2I)x = Ax - 2Ix$ $Bx = \lambda x - 2x = (\lambda - 2)x$ Step 2: Since $Bx = (\lambda - 2)x$ , this shows that $x$ is also an eigenvector of $B$ , with eigenvalue: $\lambda_B = \lambda - 2$ Final Answer: $\lambda - 2$

Solution of Laplace equation, $u(x, y)=\left(C_{1} \cos \beta x+C_{2} \sin \beta x\right)\left(C_{3} e^{\text {By }}+C_{4} e^{-\beta y}\right)$ Let square $A B C D$ is unit square. Now, given $\begin{aligned} & u(x, 0)=0 \\ & u(0, y)=0 \\ & u(1, y)=0 \\ & u(x, 1)=100 \end{aligned}$ For $u(x, 0)=0$ $\quad 0=\left(C_{1} \cos \beta x+0\right)(C_3+C_4)$ $\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{C}_{3}=-\mathrm{C}_{4}$ For $u(0, y)=0$ ; $0=\left(C_{1}+0\right)\left(C_{3} e^{\beta y}+C_{4} e^{-\beta y}\right)$ $\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{C}_{1}=0$ Now, $\begin{aligned} u(x, y) & =0+C_{2} \sin \beta x\left(C_{3} e^{\beta y}+C_{4} e^{-\beta y}\right) \\ & =a_{x} \sin \beta x\left(e^{\beta y}-e^{-\beta y}\right) \quad ...(1) \end{aligned}$ $\left[\because \mathrm{C}_{3}=-\mathrm{C}_{4}\right.$ and Let $\left.\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{C}_{3}=\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{x}}\right]$ For $u(1, y)=0$ $0=a_{x} \sin \beta x\left(e^{\beta y}-e^{\beta y}\right)$ $\Rightarrow \quad \beta=\mathrm{n} \pi$ For $u(x, 1)=100$ $a_{x} \sin n\pi x\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n \pi}\right)=100$ $a_{x}=\frac{100}{\sin n\pi x\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n \pi}\right)}$ From eqn. (1), we get $\begin{gathered} u(x, y)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{100}{\sin n \pi x\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n\pi}\right)} \times \sin n\pi x\left(e^{n \pi y}-e^{- n\pi y}\right) \\ =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{100}{\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n \pi}\right)}\left[e^{n\pi y}-e^{-n\pi y}\right] \end{gathered}$ Now, at mid point $(x, y)=\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$ $u\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)=T_{0} \text { [given] }$ $\begin{aligned} T_0&=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{100}{\left(\mathrm{e}^{n\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-n\pi}\right)}\left[\mathrm{e}^{n\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-n\pi / 2}\right] \\ &=100\left [ \left ( \frac{\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi / 2}}{\mathrm{e}^{\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}} \right ) +\left ( \frac{\mathrm{e}^{\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}}{\mathrm{e}^{2\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi}} \right )+...\right ]\\ &=100\left [ \frac{1}{(\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi / 2})}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{3\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-3\pi / 2}} +...(neglect) \right ]\\ &=100[0.199+0.043+0.008]\\ &\approx 25^{\circ}C \end{aligned}$

Let, $\begin{aligned} PQ&=C \\ P^{-1}PQ&=P^{-1}C \\ Q&=P^{-1} C\\ Q^{-1}Q&=Q^{-1}P^{-1}C \\ I&=Q^{-1}P^{-1}C \\ IC^{-1}&=Q^{-1}P^{-1}CC^{-1} \\ C^{-1}&= Q^{-1}P^{-1}\\ (PQ)^{-1}&= Q^{-1}P^{-1} \end{aligned}$ Hence, proved. Similarly, we can prove if P, Q are invertible then $(QP)^{-1}= P^{-1}Q^{-1}$

explanationHtml: Given,V=[2,3,]×[1,2]×[0,1] i.e. 2<x<3,1<y<2,0<z<1I=∭V8xyzdV=8∭VxyzdxdydzSo,=8∫x=23xdx×∫y=12ydy×∫z=01zdz=8[x22]23[y22]12[z22]01=(9−4)(4−1)(1−0)=5×3×1=15\begin{array}{l} \begin{aligned} \text{Given,}\qquad \qquad \qquad V&=[2,3,] \times[1,2] \times[0,1] \text { i.e. } \\ 2& \lt x \lt 3,1 \lt y \lt 2,0 \lt z \lt 1 \\ I&=\iiint_{V} 8 x y z d V=8 \iiint_{V} x y z d x d y d z\\ So,\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad &=8 \int_{x=2}^{3} x d x \times \int_{y=1}^{2} y d y \times \int_{z=0}^{1} z d z \\ &=8\left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{2}^{3}\left[\frac{y^{2}}{2}\right]_{1}^{2}\left[\frac{z^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=(9-4)(4-1)(1-0) \\ &=5 \times 3 \times 1 \\ &=15 \end{aligned} \end{array}Given,V2ISo,​=[2,3,]×[1,2]×[0,1] i.e. <x<3,1<y<2,0<z<1=∭V​8xyzdV=8∭V​xyzdxdydz=8∫x=23​xdx×∫y=12​ydy×∫z=01​zdz=8[2x2​]23​[2y2​]12​[2z2​]01​=(9−4)(4−1)(1−0)=5×3×1=15​​
explanationText: $\begin{array}{l} \begin{aligned} \text{Given,}\qquad \qquad \qquad V&=[2,3,] \times[1,2] \times[0,1] \text { i.e. } \\ 2& \lt x \lt 3,1 \lt y \lt 2,0 \lt z \lt 1 \\ I&=\iiint_{V} 8 x y z d V=8 \iiint_{V} x y z d x d y d z\\ So,\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad &=8 \int_{x=2}^{3} x d x \times \int_{y=1}^{2} y d y \times \int_{z=0}^{1} z d z \\ &=8\left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{2}^{3}\left[\frac{y^{2}}{2}\right]_{1}^{2}\left[\frac{z^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=(9-4)(4-1)(1-0) \\ &=5 \times 3 \times 1 \\ &=15 \end{aligned} \end{array}$

explanationHtml: V⃗=x2i^+2y3j^+z4k^▽⃗.V⃗=[∂∂xi^+∂∂yj^+∂∂zk^].[x2i^+2y3j^+z4k^]=2x+6y2+4z3At (1,2,3)▽⃗V⃗=2+6(2)2+4(3)3=134\begin{aligned} \vec{V}&=x^{2}\hat{i}+2y^{3}\hat{j}+z^{4}\hat{k} \\ \vec{\bigtriangledown }.\vec{V}&=\left [ \frac{\partial }{\partial x}\hat{i}+\frac{\partial }{\partial y}\hat{j}+\frac{\partial }{\partial z}\hat{k} \right ].\left [ x^{2}\hat{i}+2y^{3}\hat{j}+z^{4}\hat{k} \right ] \\ &=2x+6y^{2}+4z^{3}\\ &\text{At }\left ( 1,2,3 \right )\\ \vec{\bigtriangledown }\vec{V}&=2+6\left ( 2 \right )^{2}+4\left ( 3 \right )^{3} \\ &=134 \end{aligned}V▽​.V▽​V​=x2i^+2y3j^​+z4k^=[∂x∂​i^+∂y∂​j^​+∂z∂​k^].[x2i^+2y3j^​+z4k^]=2x+6y2+4z3At (1,2,3)=2+6(2)2+4(3)3=134​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \vec{V}&=x^{2}\hat{i}+2y^{3}\hat{j}+z^{4}\hat{k} \\ \vec{\bigtriangledown }.\vec{V}&=\left [ \frac{\partial }{\partial x}\hat{i}+\frac{\partial }{\partial y}\hat{j}+\frac{\partial }{\partial z}\hat{k} \right ].\left [ x^{2}\hat{i}+2y^{3}\hat{j}+z^{4}\hat{k} \right ] \\ &=2x+6y^{2}+4z^{3}\\ &\text{At }\left ( 1,2,3 \right )\\ \vec{\bigtriangledown }\vec{V}&=2+6\left ( 2 \right )^{2}+4\left ( 3 \right )^{3} \\ &=134 \end{aligned}$

explanationHtml: m=2kg,  V0=1.5 m/sec∫0tF(t)dt=m(V−V0)∫023t2dt=2(V−1.5)[t3]02=2(V−1.5)⇒    (8−0)=2(V−1.5)V=5.5 m/s \begin{aligned}m=2 kg, \; V_{0}&=1.5\: m/sec \\ \int_{0}^{t}F\left ( t \right )dt &= m\left ( V-V_{0} \right ) \\ \int_{0}^{2}3t^{2}dt &= 2\left ( V-1.5 \right ) \\ \left [ t^{3} \right ]_{0}^{2} &= 2\left ( V-1.5 \right ) \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \left ( 8-0 \right ) &= 2\left ( V-1.5 \right ) \\ V&=5.5\: m/s \end{aligned}m=2kg,V0​∫0t​F(t)dt∫02​3t2dt[t3]02​⇒(8−0)V​=1.5m/sec=m(V−V0​)=2(V−1.5)=2(V−1.5)=2(V−1.5)=5.5m/s​

=10−2=8=10-2 =8=10−2=8
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\mathrm{d} t}&=3t^{2}+1 \\ f\left ( u,\: t \right )&=3t^{2}+1 \\ u_{0}&=0 \\ t_{0}&=0 \\ \Delta t&=2\\ &\text{By Euler's method} \\ u_{1}&=u_{0}+hf\left ( u_{0}t_{0} \right ) & t_{1}&=t_{0}+h \\ &=u_{0}+h\left ( 3t^{2}_{0}+1 \right ) & &=0+2 \\ &=0+2\left ( 3\left ( 0 \right )^{2}+1 \right ) & &=2 \\ &=2 \end{aligned}$ After first iteration u=0 when t=2, $\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\mathrm{d} t}&=3t^{2}+1 \\ du&=\left ( 3t^{2}+1 \right )dt \\ \int du&=\int_{0}^{2}\left ( 3t^{2}+1 \right )dt \\ u&=\left.\begin{matrix} \left ( 3\frac{t^{3}}{3}+t \right ) \end{matrix}\right|_{0}^{2} \\ &=8+2=10 \end{aligned}$ Absolute error = Exact value - approx value $=10-2 =8$

questionText: The quadratic equation $x^{2}-4x+4=0$ is to be solved numerically, starting with the initial guess $x_0=3$ . The Newton-Raphson method is applied once to get a new estimate and then the Secant method is applied once using the initial guess and this new estimate. The estimated value of the root after the application of the Secant method is __________.
explanationHtml: f(x)=x2−4x+4f′(x)=2x−4x0=3f(3)=1,f′(3)=2By Newton Rapshon method,x1=x0−f(x0)fx0′=3−12=52f(52)=254−10+4=14By Secant method,x2=x1−(x1−x0)f(x1)f(x1)−f(x0)=f1x0−f0x1f1−f0=(14×3)−(1×52)14−1=73=2.33 \begin{aligned} f\left ( x \right )&=x^{2}-4x+4 \\ {f}'\left ( x \right )&=2x-4 \\ x_{0}&=3 \\ f\left ( 3 \right )&=1, {f}'\left ( 3 \right )=2 \\ \text{By Newton } & \text{Rapshon method,}\\ x_{1}&=x_{0}-\frac{f\left ( x_{0} \right )}{{f}'_{x_{0}}} \\ &=3-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{2} \\ f\left ( \frac{5}{2} \right )&=\frac{25}{4}-10+4=\frac{1}{4} \\ & \text{By Secant method,}\\ x_{2}&=x_{1}-\frac{\left ( x_{1}-x_{0} \right )f\left ( x_{1} \right )}{f\left ( x_{1} \right )-f\left ( x_{0} \right )} \\ &=\frac{f_{1}x_{0}-f_{0}x_{1}}{f_{1}-f_{0}} \\ &=\frac{\left ( \frac{1}{4}\times 3 \right )-\left ( 1\times \frac{5}{2} \right )}{\frac{1}{4}-1} \\ &=\frac{7}{3}=2.33 \end{aligned}f(x)f′(x)x0​f(3)By Newton x1​f(25​)x2​​=x2−4x+4=2x−4=3=1,f′(3)=2Rapshon method,=x0​−fx0​′​f(x0​)​=3−21​=25​=425​−10+4=41​By Secant method,=x1​−f(x1​)−f(x0​)(x1​−x0​)f(x1​)​=f1​−f0​f1​x0​−f0​x1​​=41​−1(41​×3)−(1×25​)​=37​=2.33​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} f\left ( x \right )&=x^{2}-4x+4 \\ {f}'\left ( x \right )&=2x-4 \\ x_{0}&=3 \\ f\left ( 3 \right )&=1, {f}'\left ( 3 \right )=2 \\ \text{By Newton } & \text{Rapshon method,}\\ x_{1}&=x_{0}-\frac{f\left ( x_{0} \right )}{{f}'_{x_{0}}} \\ &=3-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{2} \\ f\left ( \frac{5}{2} \right )&=\frac{25}{4}-10+4=\frac{1}{4} \\ & \text{By Secant method,}\\ x_{2}&=x_{1}-\frac{\left ( x_{1}-x_{0} \right )f\left ( x_{1} \right )}{f\left ( x_{1} \right )-f\left ( x_{0} \right )} \\ &=\frac{f_{1}x_{0}-f_{0}x_{1}}{f_{1}-f_{0}} \\ &=\frac{\left ( \frac{1}{4}\times 3 \right )-\left ( 1\times \frac{5}{2} \right )}{\frac{1}{4}-1} \\ &=\frac{7}{3}=2.33 \end{aligned}$
explanationTex: \begin{aligned}  f\left ( x \right )&=x^{2}-4x+4 \\   {f}'\left ( x \right )&=2x-4 \\   x_{0}&=3 \\   f\left ( 3 \right )&=1, {f}'\left ( 3 \right )=2 \\ \text{By Newton } & \text{Rapshon method,}\\   x_{1}&=x_{0}-\frac{f\left ( x_{0} \right )}{{f}'_{x_{0}}} \\    &=3-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{2} \\   f\left ( \frac{5}{2} \right )&=\frac{25}{4}-10+4=\frac{1}{4} \\ & \text{By Secant method,}\\   x_{2}&=x_{1}-\frac{\left ( x_{1}-x_{0} \right )f\left ( x_{1} \right )}{f\left ( x_{1} \right )-f\left ( x_{0} \right )} \\    &=\frac{f_{1}x_{0}-f_{0}x_{1}}{f_{1}-f_{0}} \\    &=\frac{\left ( \frac{1}{4}\times 3 \right )-\left ( 1\times \frac{5}{2} \right )}{\frac{1}{4}-1} \\    &=\frac{7}{3}=2.33 \end{aligned}

explanationText: $\begin{aligned} J&=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1\\ 2 & 4 & 2\\ 1 & 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \\ K&=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2\\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \\ K^{T}\: JK&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1\\ 2 & 4 & 2\\ 1 & 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2\\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 8 &-1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2\\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\\ &=6+16+1=23\end{aligned}$

explanationHtml: ∫−∞∞f(x)dx=1f(x)={λ(−x2+3x−2)1≤x≤20otherwise∴    ∫12λ(−x2+3x−2)dx=1⇒    λ[−x33+3x22−2x]12=1⇒    λ[−(83−13)+32(4−1)−2(2−1)]=1⇒    λ[−73+92−2]=1⇒    λ[−14+27−126]=1⇒    λ=61=6λ=6\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }f\left ( x \right )dx&=1 \\ f\left ( x \right )=\left \{ \begin{matrix} \lambda \left ( -x^{2}+3x-2 \right ) & 1\leq x\leq 2\\ 0 & otherwise \end{matrix} \right. &\\ \therefore\;\; \int_{1}^{2}\lambda \left ( -x^{2}+3x-2 \right )dx&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\frac{x^{3}}{3}+3\frac{x^{2}}{2}-2x \right ]_{1}^{2}&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\left ( \frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{3} \right )+\frac{3}{2}\left ( 4-1 \right )-2\left ( 2-1 \right ) \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\frac{7}{3}+\frac{9}{2}-2 \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ \frac{-14+27-12}{6} \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda &=\frac{6}{1}=6 \\ \lambda &=6 \end{aligned}∫−∞∞​f(x)dxf(x)={λ(−x2+3x−2)0​1≤x≤2otherwise​∴∫12​λ(−x2+3x−2)dx⇒λ[−3x3​+32x2​−2x]12​⇒λ[−(38​−31​)+23​(4−1)−2(2−1)]⇒λ[−37​+29​−2]⇒λ[6−14+27−12​]⇒λλ​=1=1=1=1=1=1=16​=6=6​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }f\left ( x \right )dx&=1 \\ f\left ( x \right )=\left \{ \begin{matrix} \lambda \left ( -x^{2}+3x-2 \right ) & 1\leq x\leq 2\\ 0 & otherwise \end{matrix} \right. &\\ \therefore\;\; \int_{1}^{2}\lambda \left ( -x^{2}+3x-2 \right )dx&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\frac{x^{3}}{3}+3\frac{x^{2}}{2}-2x \right ]_{1}^{2}&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\left ( \frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{3} \right )+\frac{3}{2}\left ( 4-1 \right )-2\left ( 2-1 \right ) \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\frac{7}{3}+\frac{9}{2}-2 \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ \frac{-14+27-12}{6} \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda &=\frac{6}{1}=6 \\ \lambda &=6 \end{aligned}$

For fff to be analysis, we have Cauchy-Riemann conditions,
∂u∂x=∂V∂y      ...(i)∂u∂y=−∂v∂x      ...(ii)From  (i) we have,6x=∂v∂y⇒  ∫∂v=∫6x∂yv=6x22+f(x)i.e., v=3x2+f(x)    ...(iii)Now applying equation (ii) we get,∂u∂y=−∂v∂x⇒    −6y=−[6x+dfdx]⇒    6x+dfdx=6ydfdx=6y−6xBy integrating,f(x)=6yx−3x2+KSubstitute in equation (iii),v=3x2+6yx−3x2+K⇒    v=6yx+K \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \;\;\;...(i) \\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \;\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{From } & \text{ (i) we have,}\\ 6x&=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \\ \Rightarrow \; \int \partial v&=\int 6x\partial y \\ v&=6\frac{x^{2}}{2}+f\left ( x \right )\\ \text{i.e., } v&=3x^{2}+f\left ( x \right )\;\;...(iii)\\ \text{Now applying }&\text{equation (ii) we get,}\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \\ \Rightarrow \; \; -6y&=-\left [ 6x+\frac{df}{dx} \right ]\\ \Rightarrow \;\; 6x+\frac{df}{dx}&=6y \\ \frac{df}{dx}&=6y-6x \\ &\text{By integrating,}\\ f\left ( x \right )&=6yx-3x^{2}+K\\ \text{Substitute }& \text{in equation (iii),}\\ v&=3x^{2}+6yx-3x^{2}+K \\ \Rightarrow \;\; v&=6yx+K \end{aligned}∂x∂u​∂y∂u​From 6x⇒∫∂vvi.e., vNow applying ∂y∂u​⇒−6y⇒6x+dxdf​dxdf​f(x)Substitute v⇒v​=∂y∂V​...(i)=−∂x∂v​...(ii) (i) we have,=∂y∂v​=∫6x∂y=62x2​+f(x)=3x2+f(x)...(iii)equation (ii) we get,=−∂x∂v​=−[6x+dxdf​]=6y=6y−6xBy integrating,=6yx−3x2+Kin equation (iii),=3x2+6yx−3x2+K=6yx+K​
explanationText: $f=u+iv \text{ and } u=3x^{2}-3y^{2}$ For $f$ to be analysis, we have Cauchy-Riemann conditions, $\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \;\;\;...(i) \\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \;\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{From } & \text{ (i) we have,}\\ 6x&=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \\ \Rightarrow \; \int \partial v&=\int 6x\partial y \\ v&=6\frac{x^{2}}{2}+f\left ( x \right )\\ \text{i.e., } v&=3x^{2}+f\left ( x \right )\;\;...(iii)\\ \text{Now applying }&\text{equation (ii) we get,}\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \\ \Rightarrow \; \; -6y&=-\left [ 6x+\frac{df}{dx} \right ]\\ \Rightarrow \;\; 6x+\frac{df}{dx}&=6y \\ \frac{df}{dx}&=6y-6x \\ &\text{By integrating,}\\ f\left ( x \right )&=6yx-3x^{2}+K\\ \text{Substitute }& \text{in equation (iii),}\\ v&=3x^{2}+6yx-3x^{2}+K \\ \Rightarrow \;\; v&=6yx+K \end{aligned}$

explanationText: The equations are, $\begin{aligned} 5x+y+2z&=34 \\ 0x+4y-3z&=12 \\ 10x-2y+z&=-4 \end{aligned}$ The augmented matrix for gauss-elimination is, $\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 5 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 4 & -3\\ 10 &-2 &1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 34\\ 12\\ -4 \end{matrix} \right ]$ Since in the first column maximum element in absolute value is 10, we need to exchange row 1 with row 3. $\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 5 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 4 & -3\\ 10 &-2 &1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 34\\ 12\\ -4 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[]{R\left ( 1,3 \right )}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 10 & -2 & 1\\ 0& 4 & -3\\ 5 & 1 & 2 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} -4\\ 12\\ 34 \end{matrix} \right ]$ So the pivot for eliminating x is $a_{11}=10$ .Now to eliminate y, we need to compass the eliminate in second column at and below the diagonal.Since $a_{22}=4$ is already larger in absolute value compares to $a_{32}=1$ $\therefore$ The pivot elementfor eliminating y is $a_{22}=4$ itself. $\therefore$ The pivots for eliminating x and y are respectively 10 and 4.

questionText: A person on a trip has a choice between private car and public transport. The probability of using a private car is 0.45. While using the public transport, further choices available are bus and metro, out of which the probability of commuting by a bus is 0.55. In such a situation, the probability (rounded up to two decimals) of using a car, bus and metro, respectively would be
explanationHtml:
Given, p(private car)=0.45
p(bus|public transport)=0.55
Since a person has a choice between private car and public transport,
p(public transport) = 1-p(private car)
=1-0.45=0.55
P(bus)=p(bus ∩\cap∩ public transport)
=p(bus|public transport) ×\times× p(public transport)
=0.55 ×\times× 0.55
=0.3025 ≃\simeq≃ 0.30
Now p(metro)=1-[p(private car)+p(bus)]
=1-(0.45+0.30)=0.25
∴\therefore∴ p(private car)=0.45

explanationHtml: y=a+bxGivenn=3, ∑x=6,∑y=21 ∑x2=14∑xy=46b=n∑xy−∑x∑yn∑x2−(∑x)2a=yˉ−bxˉ=∑yn−b∑xnSubstituting, we getb=(3×46)−(6×21)(3×14)−(6)2=2a=213−2×(63)=3∴    a=3 and b=2 \begin{aligned} y&=a+bx\\ &\text{Given}\\ n&=3,\: \sum x=6,\\ \sum y&=21\: \sum x^{2}=14\\ \sum xy&=46 \\ b&=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^{2}-\left ( \sum x \right )^{2}} \\ a&=\bar{y}-b\bar{x} \\ &=\frac{\sum y}{n}-b\frac{\sum x}{n}\\ &\text{Substituting, we get} \\ b&=\frac{\left ( 3\times 46 \right )-\left ( 6\times 21 \right )}{\left ( 3\times 14 \right )-\left ( 6 \right )^{2}}=2 \\ a&=\frac{21}{3}-2\times \left ( \frac{6}{3} \right )=3 \\ \therefore \;\; a&=3 \text{ and }b=2 \end{aligned}yn∑y∑xybaba∴a​=a+bxGiven=3,∑x=6,=21∑x2=14=46=n∑x2−(∑x)2n∑xy−∑x∑y​=yˉ​−bxˉ=n∑y​−bn∑x​Substituting, we get=(3×14)−(6)2(3×46)−(6×21)​=2=321​−2×(36​)=3=3 and b=2​

questionText: The value of $\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{x}(6-x-y)dxdy$ is
explanationHtml:
Since the limit is a function of x, we first integrate w.r.t. yyy and then w.r.t. xxx,
∫03∫0x(6−x−y)dx dy=∫03dx∫0x(6−x−y)dy=∫03dx[6y−xy−y22]0x=∫03dx(6x−x2−x22)=∫03(6x−3x22)dx=[6(x22)−32(x33)]03=[3x2−x32]03=27−272=13.5\begin{aligned}& \int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{x}\left ( 6-x-y \right )dx\: dy\\&=\int_{0}^{3}dx\int_{0}^{x}\left ( 6-x-y \right )dy \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}dx\left [ 6y-xy-\frac{y^{2}}{2} \right ]_{0}^{x} \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}dx\left ( 6x-x^{2}-\frac{x^{2}}{2} \right ) \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}\left ( 6x-\frac{3x^{2}}{2} \right )dx \\ &=\left [ 6\left ( \frac{x^{2}}{2} \right )-\frac{3}{2}\left ( \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right ) \right ]_{0}^{3} \\ &=\left [ 3x^{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{2} \right ]_{0}^{3} \\ &=27-\frac{27}{2}=13.5 \end{aligned}​∫03​∫0x​(6−x−y)dxdy=∫03​dx∫0x​(6−x−y)dy=∫03​dx[6y−xy−2y2​]0x​=∫03​dx(6x−x2−2x2​)=∫03​(6x−23x2​)dx=[6(2x2​)−23​(3x3​)]03​=[3x2−2x3​]03​=27−227​=13.5​
explanationText: Since the limit is a function of x, we first integrate w.r.t. $y$ and then w.r.t. $x$ , $\begin{aligned}& \int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{x}\left ( 6-x-y \right )dx\: dy\\&=\int_{0}^{3}dx\int_{0}^{x}\left ( 6-x-y \right )dy \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}dx\left [ 6y-xy-\frac{y^{2}}{2} \right ]_{0}^{x} \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}dx\left ( 6x-x^{2}-\frac{x^{2}}{2} \right ) \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}\left ( 6x-\frac{3x^{2}}{2} \right )dx \\ &=\left [ 6\left ( \frac{x^{2}}{2} \right )-\frac{3}{2}\left ( \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right ) \right ]_{0}^{3} \\ &=\left [ 3x^{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{2} \right ]_{0}^{3} \\ &=27-\frac{27}{2}=13.5 \end{aligned}$

questionText: For what values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ the following simultaneous equations have an infinite number of solutions ? x + y + z = 5; x + 3y + 3z = 9; x + 2y + $\alpha$ z = $\beta$
explanationHtml:
The augmented matrix for this system is,
[11113312α∣59β]\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 &1 \\ 1& 3 & 3\\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{matrix}\right| \begin{matrix} 5\\ 9\\ \beta \end{matrix}\right ]​111​132​13α​​59β​​
Using Gauss-elimination method we get
[11113312α∣59β]→R3−R1→R2−R1[11102201α−1∣54β−5]→R3−12R2[11102200α−2∣54β−7]\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 &1 \\ 1& 3 & 3\\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{matrix}\right| \begin{matrix} 5\\ 9\\ \beta \end{matrix}\right ]\xrightarrow[R_{3}-R_{1}]{\overset{R_{2}-R_{1}}{\rightarrow}}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2 & 2\\ 0 & 1 & \alpha -1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 5\\ 4\\ \beta -5 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[]{R_{3}-\frac{1}{2}R_{2}}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & \alpha -2 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 5\\ 4\\ \beta -7 \end{matrix} \right ]​111​132​13α​​59β​​→R2​−R1​R3​−R1​​​100​121​12α−1​​54β−5​​R3​−21​R2​​​100​120​12α−2​​54β−7​​
Now, for infinite solution last row must be completely zero
i.e. α−2\alpha -2α−2 and β−7=0\beta -7=0β−7=0
⇒      α=2\Rightarrow \;\;\; \alpha =2⇒α=2 and β=7\beta =7β=7
explanationText: The augmented matrix for this system is, $\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 &1 \\ 1& 3 & 3\\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{matrix}\right| \begin{matrix} 5\\ 9\\ \beta \end{matrix}\right ]$ Using Gauss-elimination method we get $\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 &1 \\ 1& 3 & 3\\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{matrix}\right| \begin{matrix} 5\\ 9\\ \beta \end{matrix}\right ]\xrightarrow[R_{3}-R_{1}]{\overset{R_{2}-R_{1}}{\rightarrow}}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2 & 2\\ 0 & 1 & \alpha -1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 5\\ 4\\ \beta -5 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[]{R_{3}-\frac{1}{2}R_{2}}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & \alpha -2 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 5\\ 4\\ \beta -7 \end{matrix} \right ]$ Now, for infinite solution last row must be completely zeroi.e. $\alpha -2$ and $\beta -7=0$ $\Rightarrow \;\;\; \alpha =2$ and $\beta =7$

explanationText: Green's theorem is, $\begin{aligned} \oint_{c} \phi dx + \Psi dy&=\int_{E}\left ( \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial x}-\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial x} \right )\: dxdy\\ \text{Here } I&=\oint_{c} \left ( xydy\: -\: y^{2}dx \right ) \\ &=\oint_{c} \left ( -y^{2} \right )dx\: +\: \left ( xy \right )dy \\ \therefore \;\; \phi &=-y^{2},\; \Psi = xy \\ \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial x}&=y,\; \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial y}=-2y\end{aligned}$ Substituting in Green's Theorem, we get, $\begin{aligned} I&= \int_{y=0}^{1}\int_{x=0}^{1}\left [ y-\left ( -2y \right ) \right ]dx\: dy \\ &= \int_{y=0}^{1}\int_{x=0}^{1}\: 3y\: dx\: dy \\ &= \int_{y=0}^{1}\left [ 3xy \right ]_{x=0}^{1}\: dy \\ &= \int_{y=0}^{1}3ydy=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$

(D) is true since
∣Z1+Z2∣2=(Z1+Z2)(Z1+Z2‾)=(Z1+Z2)(Z1ˉ+Z2ˉ)=Z1Z1ˉ+Z2Z2ˉ+Z2Z1ˉ+Z1Z2ˉ    ...(i)∣Z1−Z2∣2=(Z1+Z2)(Z1−Z2‾)=(Z1−Z2)(Z1ˉ−Z2ˉ)=Z1Z1ˉ+Z2Z2ˉ−Z2Z1ˉ−Z1Z2ˉ    ...(ii) \begin{aligned}\left | Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right |^{2}&=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \overline{Z_{1}+Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \bar{Z_{1}}+\bar{Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=Z_{1}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}} \;\;...(i)\\ \left | Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right |^{2}&=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \overline{Z_{1}-Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=\left ( Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right )\left ( \bar{Z_{1}}-\bar{Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=Z_{1}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}-Z_{2}\bar{Z_{1}}-Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}\;\;...(ii)\end{aligned}∣Z1​+Z2​∣2∣Z1​−Z2​∣2​=(Z1​+Z2​)(Z1​+Z2​​)=(Z1​+Z2​)(Z1​ˉ​+Z2​ˉ​)=Z1​Z1​ˉ​+Z2​Z2​ˉ​+Z2​Z1​ˉ​+Z1​Z2​ˉ​...(i)=(Z1​+Z2​)(Z1​−Z2​​)=(Z1​−Z2​)(Z1​ˉ​−Z2​ˉ​)=Z1​Z1​ˉ​+Z2​Z2​ˉ​−Z2​Z1​ˉ​−Z1​Z2​ˉ​...(ii)​

S is an arithmetico-geometric series and can be summed up as follows,
S=2+(52+822)+1123+...∞)=2+x    (say)where x=52+822+1123+...∞    ...(i)Multiplying by 1/2, we get, 12x=522+823+1124+...∞    ...(ii)Substracting (ii) from (i), we get, x−12x=52+(8−5)22+(11−8)23+(13−11)24+...∞x2=52+(322+323+324+...∞)x2=52+322[1−12]x2=52+32=4∴    x=8and S=2+x=10 \begin{aligned} S&=2+\left ( \frac{5}{2}+\frac{8}{2^{2})}+\frac{11}{2^{3}}+...\infty \right ) \\ &=2+x\;\; (say)\\ \text{where } x&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{8}{2^{2}}+\frac{11}{2^{3}}+...\infty \;\; ...(i)\\ \text{Multiplying by }&\text{1/2, we get, } \\ \frac{1}{2}x&=\frac{5}{2^{2}}+\frac{8}{2^{3}}+\frac{11}{2^{4}}+...\infty \;\;...(ii) \\ \text{Substracting (ii) } & \text{from (i), we get, }\\ x-\frac{1}{2}x&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{\left ( 8-5 \right )}{2^{2}} \\ &+\frac{\left ( 11-8 \right )}{2^{3}} +\frac{\left ( 13-11 \right )}{2^{4}}+...\infty \\ \frac{x}{2}&=\frac{5}{2}+\left ( \frac{3}{2^{2}}+\frac{3}{2^{3}}+\frac{3}{2^{4}}+...\infty \right ) \\ \frac{x}{2}&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{\frac{3}{2^{2}}}{\left [ 1-\frac{1}{2} \right ]} \\ \frac{x}{2}&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=4 \\ \therefore \;\; x&=8\\ \text{and } S&=2+x=10\end{aligned}Swhere xMultiplying by 21​xSubstracting (ii) x−21​x2x​2x​2x​∴xand S​=2+(25​+22)8​+2311​+...∞)=2+x(say)=25​+228​+2311​+...∞...(i)1/2, we get, =225​+238​+2411​+...∞...(ii)from (i), we get, =25​+22(8−5)​+23(11−8)​+24(13−11)​+...∞=25​+(223​+233​+243​+...∞)=25​+[1−21​]223​​=25​+23​=4=8=2+x=10​
explanationText: S is an arithmetico-geometric series and can be summed up as follows, $\begin{aligned} S&=2+\left ( \frac{5}{2}+\frac{8}{2^{2})}+\frac{11}{2^{3}}+...\infty \right ) \\ &=2+x\;\; (say)\\ \text{where } x&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{8}{2^{2}}+\frac{11}{2^{3}}+...\infty \;\; ...(i)\\ \text{Multiplying by }&\text{1/2, we get, } \\ \frac{1}{2}x&=\frac{5}{2^{2}}+\frac{8}{2^{3}}+\frac{11}{2^{4}}+...\infty \;\;...(ii) \\ \text{Substracting (ii) } & \text{from (i), we get, }\\ x-\frac{1}{2}x&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{\left ( 8-5 \right )}{2^{2}} \\ &+\frac{\left ( 11-8 \right )}{2^{3}} +\frac{\left ( 13-11 \right )}{2^{4}}+...\infty \\ \frac{x}{2}&=\frac{5}{2}+\left ( \frac{3}{2^{2}}+\frac{3}{2^{3}}+\frac{3}{2^{4}}+...\infty \right ) \\ \frac{x}{2}&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{\frac{3}{2^{2}}}{\left [ 1-\frac{1}{2} \right ]} \\ \frac{x}{2}&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=4 \\ \therefore \;\; x&=8\\ \text{and } S&=2+x=10\end{aligned}$

questionText: A box contains 10 screws, 3 of which are defective. Two screws are drawn at random with replacement. The probability that none of the two screws is defective will be

options.html: None of these

explanationHtml:
Total number of screws = 10
Number of defective screws = 3
Number of non-defective screws = 10−3=710 - 3 = 710−3=7

Probability of selecting a non-defective screw in one draw:
P(non-defective)=710P(\text{non-defective}) = \frac{7}{10}P(non-defective)=107​

Since the screws are drawn with replacement, the two events are independent. So, the probability that both screws drawn are non-defective is:
P(both non-defective)=(710)2=49100=0.49 P(\text{both non-defective}) = \left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^2 = \frac{49}{100} = 0.49 P(both non-defective)=(107​)2=10049​=0.49

Hence, the required probability is 49%.
explanationText: Total number of screws = 10 Number of defective screws = 3 Number of non-defective screws = $10 - 3 = 7$ Probability of selecting a non-defective screw in one draw: $P(\text{non-defective}) = \frac{7}{10}$ Since the screws are drawn with replacement, the two events are independent. So, the probability that both screws drawn are non-defective is: $P(\text{both non-defective}) = \left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^2 = \frac{49}{100} = 0.49$ Hence, the required probability is 49%.

explanationText: Consider first $3\times 3$ minors, since maximum possible rank is 3 $\begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 2 &1 \\ 6 & 3 & 4\\ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 &3 \\ 3 & 4& 7\\ 1 & 0& 1 \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 1 & 3\\ 6 & 4 & 7\\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}&=0\\ \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 2 &3 \\ 6 & 3 & 7\\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}&=0 \end{aligned}$ Since all $3\times 3$ minors are zero, now try $2\times 2$ minors. $\begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} 4 &2 \\ 6 & 3 \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ \begin{vmatrix} 2 &1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix}&=8-3=5\neq 0 \\ \therefore\;\; \text{rank }&=2 \end{aligned}$
